Теории достаточно — перейдём к примеру.

Предположим, завтра у вас важный экзамен в учёбе или на работе, и приходит мысль: «Я провалю экзамен».

Гарантий исхода нет, но мысль уже тревожит. Значит, дадим мозгу альтернативы.

Самый худший: я плохо подготовлюсь, на экзамене растеряюсь и не сдам. Хуже того — окажусь единственным в группе, кто не справился. Преподаватель разочаруется, а одногруппники решат, что я ленив и несобран.

Самый лучший: спокойно приеду на экзамен, попаду на лёгкий билет и сдам на «отлично». А ещё лучше — если всей группе поставят высшие баллы без экзамена.

Самый реалистичный: я не знаю, какой билет попадётся, но могу сегодня повторить сложные темы — так завтра будет спокойнее. Лёгкое волнение — нормально. В целом материал я знаю и на большинство вопросов смогу ответить. Преподаватель ко мне настроен доброжелательно, причин «заваливать» нет. Утром освежу проблемные места и буду увереннее. Скорее всего, сдам минимум на «удовлетворительно», а при собранности — на «хорошо» или «отлично».

<q author="Виктор Франкл">Между стимулом и реакцией есть пространство. В этом пространстве — наша свобода выбирать ответ. В выборе ответа — наш рост и наша свобода.</q>
en.oldText:
That’s enough theory — let’s move on to an example.

Imagine you have an important exam tomorrow — at university or at work — and the thought comes: “I’m going to fail the exam.”

There are no guarantees about the outcome yet, but the thought is already making you anxious. So let’s give your brain some alternatives.

Worst case: I’ll prepare badly, get confused during the exam and fail it. Even worse — I’ll be the only one in the group who doesn’t pass. The lecturer will be disappointed, and my classmates will decide I’m lazy and disorganized.

Best case: I’ll calmly arrive at the exam, get an easy question and pass with the highest grade. Or even better — the whole group will get top marks without having to sit the exam at all.

Most realistic: I don’t know which question I’ll get, but today I can review the more difficult topics so I feel calmer tomorrow. A bit of nervousness is normal. Overall I know the material and will be able to answer most of the questions. The lecturer is generally well-disposed towards me and has no reason to “fail” me on purpose. In the morning I’ll go over the trickier parts again and feel more confident. Most likely I’ll pass at least with a satisfactory grade, and if I stay focused — with a good or even an excellent one.
en.newText:
Enough theory — let’s look at an example.

Suppose you have an important exam at school or work tomorrow, and the thought pops up: “I’m going to fail.”

There’s no guarantee of the outcome, but the thought is already causing anxiety. So, let’s give your brain some alternatives.

The absolute worst: I won’t prepare well, I’ll panic during the exam, and I’ll fail. Even worse — I’ll be the only one in the group who didn’t make it. The instructor will be disappointed, and my classmates will think I’m lazy and disorganized.

The absolute best: I’ll arrive at the exam calmly, get an easy topic, and ace it. Even better — if the whole group gets top marks without even having to take the exam.

The most realistic: I don’t know which topic I’ll get, but I can review the difficult subjects today — that will make me feel calmer tomorrow. A little nervousness is normal. Overall, I know the material and can answer most questions. The instructor is friendly toward me, and there’s no reason to fail. I’ll refresh my knowledge on the tricky parts in the morning and feel more confident. Most likely, I’ll pass with at least a satisfactory grade, and if I stay focused, I’ll get a good or excellent grade.

This approach gives you at least three possible outcomes — and in reality there are usually even more.

It’s helpful to think through a “backup plan” in advance for the worst-case scenario.

This significantly lowers the emotional intensity: even if the worst does happen, you’ll already have an idea of how to respond.

For example: if I really do fail the exam tomorrow, I’ll have a chance to retake it. It’s unpleasant, but I can set aside another day or two to prepare and put things right.

It’s unlikely that the lecturer’s and my classmates’ attitude toward me will radically change because of one failure; and if it does, that will simply show how much their opinion is really worth.

Looking at things this way, the situation no longer seems so frightening, and the thought no longer feels like the only option.

At first it may seem either too simple or, on the contrary, too time-consuming to write all this out.

But practice shows: this technique really works as a self-help tool — and that’s exactly why we’re offering it to you.

В КПТ есть много простых и полезных приёмов для работы с негативными автоматическими мыслями. Одни техники помогают замечать такие мысли, другие — проверять их на здравый смысл и снижать доверие к ним. Большинство упражнений можно выполнять самостоятельно, чтобы поддерживать своё состояние. В этой главе мы поделимся инструментом, который отлично справляется с зацикливанием на одной мысли. Это техника «Три варианта развития событий». Если вы уже научились ловить мысли, которые сильно задевают, вы, скорее всего, заметили: многие из них иррациональны и плохо соотносятся с фактами — но мы всё равно склонны им верить и не всегда понимаем, как с ними обходиться. Главная задача техники — расширить поле зрения и показать психике, что помимо тревожного сценария есть и другие. В процессе работы вы научитесь сомневаться в негативных мыслях и снижать тревогу в стрессовых ситуациях. Что делать? Схема простая. Как только вы заметили мысль, которая испортила настроение, задайте себе вопрос: как могут развиваться события?
  • Худший — самый неприятный вариант, который обычно первым приходит в голову;
  • Лучший — идеальный исход, который вас полностью устроил бы;
  • Реалистичный — середина между первым и вторым: взвешенный сценарий, опирающийся на опыт и факты;
    • Важная деталь: варианты лучше не держать в голове, а записывать. Это можно сделать в телефоне или на бумаге — как удобнее. Запись помогает взглянуть на ситуацию трезвее.
en.oldText:
CBT offers many simple and useful tools for working with negative automatic thoughts.

Some techniques help you notice these thoughts, others test them against common sense so you gradually trust them less. Most exercises can be done on your own to support your emotional state. In this chapter we’ll share a tool that works especially well when you get stuck on a single thought. It’s called the “Three Possible Outcomes” technique.

If you’ve already learned to catch the thoughts that really hurt, you’ve probably noticed: many of them are irrational and poorly aligned with the facts — yet we still tend to believe them and don’t always know what to do with them.

The main goal of this technique is to widen your field of view and show your mind that, besides the anxious scenario, there are other options. As you practice, you’ll learn to question negative thoughts and lower your anxiety in stressful situations.

What do you do? The structure is simple. As soon as you notice a thought that spoils your mood, ask yourself: how could events unfold?

Worst case — the most unpleasant option, which usually comes to mind first;

Best case — the ideal outcome that would fully satisfy you;

Realistic — something in between the first and the second: a balanced scenario grounded in experience and facts.

An important detail: it’s better not to keep these options in your head, but to write them down. You can do this on your phone or on paper — whatever is more convenient. Putting things in writing helps you look at the situation more soberly.
en.newText:
CBT offers many simple and useful tools for working with negative automatic thoughts. Some techniques help you notice these thoughts, while others help you check them for logic and reduce how much you believe them. Most exercises can be done on your own to help maintain your mental well-being. In this chapter, we’ll share a tool that is excellent for breaking the cycle of rumination. It’s called the “Three Options” technique. If you’ve already learned to catch thoughts that hit hard, you’ve likely noticed that many of them are irrational and don’t align with the facts—yet we still tend to believe them and don’t always know how to handle them. The main goal of this technique is to broaden your perspective and show your mind that there are other possibilities beyond the anxious scenario. Through this process, you’ll learn to question negative thoughts and reduce anxiety in stressful situations. So, what do you do? The scheme is simple. As soon as you notice a thought that has ruined your mood, ask yourself: how could things play out?
  • The worst — the most unpleasant option, which is usually the first one that comes to mind;
  • The best — the ideal outcome that would satisfy you completely;
  • The most realistic — the middle ground between the first two: a balanced scenario based on experience and facts;
    • A key detail: it’s better to write these scenarios down rather than just keeping them in your head. You can do this on your phone or on paper — whichever is more convenient. Writing them down helps you look at the situation more objectively.
